Forty Sensors on the Varn Glacier Start Listening

A three-summer effort to wire the ice is complete, and the first recordings are already in.

Ingrid Solberg · 3 October 2026

Researchers at the University of Tarn have finished installing forty seismic sensors along the Varn glacier, a project that took three summers and two helicopters. The array listens for the faint cracking that happens when meltwater forces its way under the ice.

Each sensor sits in a shallow borehole, sealed with a plug of frozen slush, and reports to a solar-powered relay on the ridge. The team chose the sites by hand, walking the glacier with ice axes and a printed map, because satellite images could not show which crevasses were safe to cross.

Advertisement

“We expected the ice to be quiet in winter, but it never really stops,” said Dr. Henrik Aas, who leads the project. He said the first month of data shows small bursts of activity almost every night, often just after the temperature drops below minus fifteen.

The data will be published openly, and the group plans to compare it with records from two smaller glaciers in the same valley. If the patterns match, the method could give early warning of sudden floods, which have damaged roads and farms downstream three times in the last decade.

Funding for the next phase, which would add thirty more sensors and a winter maintenance crew, has not yet been approved. A decision is expected in the spring, the university said.
